newsitem.title: CHINA: N.Korea defector languishes amid S.Korea-China row.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea defector languishes amid S.Korea-China row.

text.p: A North Korean defector languished on Monday in his fifth week in a diplomatic limbo in the South Korean mission in Seoul, surrounded by heavy Chinese security but with a possible end in sight to his ordeal.

Rumours swirled that Hwang Jang-yop, the highest level official ever to betray his Stalinist homeland, had left or was about to leave Seoul's consulate in Beijing and would fly to Seoul via a third country -- possibly the Philippines.

But at the end of the day Hwang remained out of sight, still inside the mission in the sedate diplomatic quarter of Beijing that was sealed off by dozens of Chinese police armed with assault rifles and backed by armoured personnel carriers in case North Korean attempts to recover its top ideologue.

Three vans seen driving away in the early hours of Monday, following a visit to the consulate by South Korean ambassador Chung Chong-wook on Sunday night, touched off a false alarm, one Seoul official said.
"Hwang Jang-yop will be able to leave China this week but his departure might not be today or tomorrow," a senior foreign ministry official, who declined to be identified, told reporters in Seoul.
"He will have to stay in a third country for a considerable period of time before coming to South Korea," he said.
A South Korea embassy spokesman in Beijing attributed the main sticking point preventing Hwang's departure to a dispute with Beijing over where Hwang should be taken.
"In principle we want to bring him to Korea but... we may have to find another way," said spokesman Chang Moon-ik.

"It could be this week, it could be next week," Chang said when asked when Hwang, Korea's top ideologue and senior aide to supreme leader Kim Jong-il, would leave Beijing. He sought refuge at the consular compound in Beijing on February 12.

China's Foreign Ministry refused to comment on Hwang's fate, saying they could report no new developments since Premier Li Peng said last Friday that conditions were nearly ripe for a solution to the diplomatic crisis.
The defection of Hwang, the most senior official to abandon his Stalinist homeland, has muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War.
Beijing must decide whether to hand over Hwang to new business partner Seoul while giving full consideration to the concerns of old communist ally Pyongyang.
Officials have said the Philippines was one of several transit points being considered.
Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Saturday his country had been asked to serve as such a transit point if Hwang were allowed to leave for South Korea.
Siazon, on a five-day visit to Tokyo, said that some other routes besides the Philippines were probably being considered.
A top Manila Foreign Office official said Hwang would very likely stay in the Philippines for a few days, but added that it was possible his country was being used as a decoy.
Hwang, a close aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, is ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy.
He is credited with devising the national creed of "juche", which stresses self-reliance and has kept North Korea frozen in Stalinist-era isolation and economic backwardness.
